title: What tool can find customer quotes about specific sales objections?
summary: Find useful sales quotes in customer interviews by topic, then turn the strongest answers into source-linked clips your video editor can use.
body_markdown:
## What you’ll take away


- Search for the customer's experience behind an objection, not only the sales team's keyword.
- Choose a complete answer with its qualifications, rather than the most enthusiastic phrase.
- Give the editor usable source moments and keep publishing approval separate.


## Start with the objection as a real question


“Find ROI quotes” is a weak brief because ROI can mean money, time, avoided work, or confidence in a decision. Translate it into the question the prospect is asking. “Will implementation disrupt my team?” calls for a different answer from “How quickly did you recover the cost?” A quote that answers one should not be presented as evidence for the other.


For an illustrative project, imagine six customer interviews from a recent shoot. Sales needs short videos addressing setup effort, adoption by skeptical colleagues, and whether the product fits an existing workflow. Those are three search topics, not a request to generate three favorable claims. A useful result can also tell you that one topic was never discussed.


## Choose a search tool rather than a collection form


If customers have not recorded their answers yet, begin with an interview or collection workflow. If the interviews exist but no one can find the right moments, you need source search. If approved clips already exist and sales cannot locate them, you may need a better library and tagging process. Buying another editing tool will not resolve unclear access or ownership of finished assets.


Wideframe's[find-soundbites workflow](https://try.wideframe.com/skills/find-soundbites/) is documented for topic-based, timecoded selections. That makes it relevant to the second situation: turning existing recordings into candidate evidence. It is not a substitute for a system that records customer consent, approves commercial claims, or controls sales-team distribution.


To begin in Wideframe, point a chat at the customer interview folder and give it the objection topics. The linked soundbite recipe can be pasted into a new chat to add and save this task for future source searches.


## Give each topic a useful definition


Tell the assistant what qualifies and what does not. For setup effort, qualifying passages might describe the steps taken, people involved, and interruptions encountered. Generic praise such as “the team was great” may be pleasant but does not answer implementation risk. Ask for more than one candidate when the source supports it, so you can choose between different levels of detail.


Include likely customer vocabulary. A speaker may describe “getting everyone onto the new process” without ever saying “adoption.” Explain that relationship in the request. Keep the customer's own words in the returned material; the sales team's wording belongs in your topic label, not inside quotation marks.


## Pick the answer that a skeptical buyer can use


Review the candidate with the question that prompted it. A claim about one pilot group can become misleading if the edit implies a company-wide rollout. Preserve words that define scope, timing, uncertainty, and responsibility. A longer qualified answer often provides more useful evidence than a short, sweeping endorsement.


Choose for relevance before enthusiasm. A calm explanation of how a team handled onboarding may answer an objection better than a delighted “we love it.” Keep contrasting or unresolved experiences visible in your internal notes. The job is to find credible customer evidence, not force every recording into the same success story.


## Make an editor-ready answer, not a pile of quotes


Give each chosen clip a purpose: the buyer question it answers, a source location, and the minimal context needed on screen. A useful short edit might begin with a plain heading such as “What onboarding involved,” identify the customer, and let a complete answer play. Add product footage only if it illustrates the process being discussed.


For a Premiere-based team, take approved selections through Wideframe's[Premiere export workflow](https://try.wideframe.com/skills/export-premiere/) and finish the sequence there. Keep the original interview available so the editor can extend a boundary or restore context. Source-linked selects make that revision practical; a copied quotation in a slide deck does not.


## Package the clips for the sales conversation


Name the finished assets by the question they answer, not just the customer name. Include a short internal description of the audience, the claim's scope, and when not to use the clip. Keep approval status visible in whatever library your team already uses. Do not treat an edited candidate as an approved sales asset.


Separate editorial captions from the speaker's words. A heading may explain the question, while captions represent the actual answer. If the footage does not contain a usable answer, commission a follow-up question or use another form of evidence. An AI assistant should not supply testimony that the customer never gave.


## Return when the next objection changes


After the next customer interview, search the same recurring topic list and add genuinely new evidence. Also listen to the sales team: if prospects begin asking about a different integration or workflow, that creates a new research question for the archive.


Save the useful topic definitions and output preferences as recurring instructions. Refresh the inputs and approval information each time. The repeatable value is finding the right source moment when a buyer question changes, while keeping the customer's meaning intact.


## Try this request


TRY AN EXAMPLE REQUEST


Find customer interview answers about setup effort, team adoption, and fitting into an existing workflow. Give me up to three complete answers per topic with source timecodes. Favor specific experiences over generic praise, preserve qualifications, and say when a topic is not covered.

## Frequently asked questions


Describe the experience you mean and include likely phrasing. Review the candidates in context; thematic relevance is an editorial judgment, not proof of the business claim.


Usually the editor and approver should see candidates first. Give sales clearly approved clips with a description of the question each answers.


Record the gap and ask an actual customer a follow-up question. Do not turn an adjacent quote into a stronger answer than it supports.
